messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Keoni had been six years old the first time his father’s lighter clicked near his skin. The flame never touched him directly—his father was too clever for that—but the stench of singed cotton and melting nylon from his own shirt had seared itself into his memory. That smell meant he had done something wrong again, meant his father’s hand would follow the flame, meant he would be held down until he stopped crying. By the time Keoni turned nine, he had learned to keep his face flat and his voice low, because any flicker of happiness was a provocation. A smile meant he was getting too comfortable, and comfort was a crime. So he buried every good feeling before it could show, and the habit never left him.

Now, at fifty-six, Keoni worked as a detective in a medium-sized city. The job had seemed like a natural fit when he was younger—he was watchful, could read a room without being read, and had a memory for details others missed. But the same vigilance that made him good at his work had turned into a constant, grinding hyperarousal. He could not sit with his back to a door. He could not sleep through the night because his body insisted on staying alert, listening for footsteps that never came. When a child-victim case crossed his desk, he would study the photographs with a clenched jaw, seeing not a stranger’s face but his own small, terrified reflection. He would push the file away and mutter about needing coffee, but the rage was already building—a hot, wordless fury that left him shaking and unable to focus on the next page. That rage was the only emotion that ever felt clean. Positive emotions, the rare moments of genuine warmth or contentment, filled him with an unnamed dread, as if they were a trap waiting to snap shut.

Keoni had come to believe that the abuse had happened because of who he was. He was a lousy coper, he told himself—look at how he still flinched at a burnt match, how his hands would tremble when he passed a man wearing a certain style of work shirt. He had stopped wearing button-downs himself, and he avoided the grocery store after five o’clock because too many fathers came in straight from construction jobs, their clothes smelling of sweat and smoke. He had also learned to detach from the memories when they surfaced, to step outside his own mind and watch the scene from a distance. The problem was that they often surfaced without warning—a whiff of something acrid on the street, and suddenly he was back in the kitchen, pinned on the linoleum, the lighter clicking again. He could never explain what had happened in those moments; when he tried to tell a colleague or even his ex-wife, his thoughts would dissolve into a tangle of fragments, and he would trail off mid-sentence, unable to finish.

The divorce had been quiet and final. His wife had said he was never really there, that he had stopped letting her in years ago. She was right. Avoidance had become his default. He kept his social circle small, then nonexistent. He worked late into the night, alone in his office, because there were fewer people to watch. The hypervigilance never rested, but at least when he was alone, no one could notice the way he scanned every corner of a room.

What finally brought Keoni to the clinic was a case three weeks earlier. He had been called to a house fire that had killed a child. The smell of burnt insulation and melted plastics had hit him before he even stepped out of the car. He had frozen on the sidewalk, his heart hammering, his vision tunneling. For a long minute he had not known where or when he was. A younger officer had touched his elbow, asking if he was okay, and Keoni had snapped at him, then retreated to his car and driven home without a word. The next morning, his captain told him he was taking mandatory leave and gave him a list of therapists approved for department referrals. Keoni had taken the list because refusing would have raised more questions, but he still was not sure he could sit in a room and tell a stranger the whole story—especially because he was certain that once he started, he would not be able to explain it clearly, and the stranger would see exactly what kind of person he really was.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Shattered Beliefs: The vignette does not describe that the patient's beliefs about how the world works were completely destroyed; it only mentions self-blame and hypervigilance.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

By the time he was twelve, he had come to see the world as a place where danger lurked in every smile, where kindness was a mask for cruelty, and where no amount of caution could ever guarantee safety. The hypervigilance never rested, but at least when he was alone, no one could notice the way he scanned every corner of a room. Even now, he was certain that the world was fundamentally dangerous—that no one could really be trusted, that safety was a lie people told themselves. That was why he never let anyone close. That was why, when a colleague offered help, he saw a threat.

The smell of burnt insulation and melted plastics had hit him before he even stepped out of the car. He had frozen on the sidewalk, his heart hammering, his vision tunneling. For a long minute he had not known where or when he was. A younger officer had touched his elbow, asking if he was okay, and Keoni had snapped at him, then retreated to his car and driven home without a word. Keoni had taken the list because refusing would have raised more questions, but he still was not sure he could sit in a room and tell a stranger the whole story—especially because he was certain that once he started, he would not be able to explain it clearly, and the stranger would see exactly what kind of person he really was.
